ideas.title: Independent audit desk for city surveillance vendors
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price monthly service that checks whether a city's license-plate-reader and drone vendor is actually following the city's own sharing rules, and hands the council a report it can cite.
ideas.customer: City auditors, city attorneys and city managers (plus police oversight boards) in the roughly 50+ cities that cancelled or suspended Flock and the many more that kept ALPR or drone programs under new council conditions. Buyers pay $1.2k-2.5k/month per city from the auditor, city attorney or IT budget, well under the informal-procurement threshold.
ideas.problem: Cities cannot verify what the surveillance vendor does with their data. Mountain View's own audit found a statewide-lookup setting active on 29 of 30 cameras since program start, with 250+ outside agencies running about 600,000 searches in 12 months, and the vendor kept no records that would show what was shared. Oxnard's vendor silently re-enabled a nationwide query feature. Evanston found cameras reinstalled after cancellation. Dayton found 7,100+ searches for immigration enforcement that city policy prohibited. Councils now write audit duties into ordinances, but the auditor's office has no tooling.
ideas.solution: A vendor-neutral audit service (Flock, Axon, Motorola/Vigilant, drone platforms). The city exports the search and audit logs and sharing-settings screenshots it can already download. The service ingests them and runs a rules engine against the city's adopted policy: searches with no case number or with vague reason codes, out-of-state or federal agencies, immigration-related terms, off-hours spikes, and diffs of the network-sharing settings month to month to catch silent config changes. Output is a council-ready quarterly report and a same-week alert on config drift. Add-on: a field check that cameras a council ordered off are really off, since Evanston found them reinstalled.
ideas.why_now: 53 cities across 20 states had cancelled or rejected Flock by mid-2026 over unauthorized federal access. New state laws (Colorado SB 26-070 warrant rule, Washington SB 6002, Kentucky HB 58 90-day retention cap, Maine's ALPR law) add compliance duties. Atlanta's ordinance, held in committee and taken up again in September 2026, would require monthly internal access audits and annual independent technical audits managed by the City Auditor. Drone-as-first-responder approvals (Stockton, Federal Way, Santa Fe, Whittier) are expanding the audit surface.
ideas.revenue_model: $4.5k one-time baseline configuration and log audit, then $1.2k-2.5k/month monitoring and quarterly council report. Upsell: annual independent technical audit that ordinances like Atlanta's require, priced $15k-40k for larger cities. Multi-year contracts through city auditor offices.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The market is created by oversight ordinances, not by the surveillance vendors. Every ordinance that says 'audit monthly' is an unfunded mandate on a three-person auditor's office, and the failure mode is configuration drift, not sophisticated data science. Evidence: Mountain View's statewide lookup ran from launch until Jan 5, 2026 unnoticed (https://www.mv-voice.com/police/2026/01/30/amid-immigration-crackdown-mountain-view-discovers-unauthorized-access-to-license-plate-data/). The audit findings and 53-city cancellation count are in https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319317/20260629/flock-safety-crosses-100000-cameras-53-cities-cancel-over-unauthorized-federal-data-access.htm. Atlanta's proposed monthly internal and annual independent audits are at https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/09/22/atlanta-weighs-sweeping-rules-monthly-audits-surveillance-tech/. New Hanover County's commissioners called for 'explicit guardrails' before restoring cameras: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9840468/north-carolina/new-hanover-county/commissioners-cite-privacy-shifting-vendor-policies-and-misuse-when-cancelling-flock-alpr-contract. Cities that keep the cameras need proof of compliance to survive the next council vote, and the audit report is that proof.
ideas.first_30_days: File public-records requests in about 25 cities that cancelled or kept ALPR for the audit-log export format and sharing-settings history, and build a parser for it. Produce one free 'configuration drift' teardown for a friendly city attorney or a councilmember who championed the cancellation. Pitch the $4.5k baseline audit to auditors and attorneys in cities with surveillance-oversight ordinances (Seattle, San Diego, Oakland, Cambridge, Urbana) and to those now drafting them (Atlanta). Sign 3 pilots. Main risk: vendor cooperation and export formats, so start with cities that already run their own audits.

ideas.title: Sole-source price-reasonableness memos from council agenda data
ideas.one_liner: A buy-side benchmark built from public council packets showing what other governments pay Tyler, Axon, OpenGov and Flock, sold as the missing price-reasonableness memo for every sole-source renewal.
ideas.customer: Finance directors, IT directors, purchasing officers and clerks in cities and counties of 5k-250k renewing proprietary software (ERP, permitting, body cameras, ALPR). They pay $495-$1,500 per renewal brief or $3k/year subscription. Councilmembers who want a sanity check are the second audience.
ideas.problem: Vendors keep pricing confidential, and sole-source renewals sail through with no comparison. Steuben County, NY approved a five-year Tyler MUNIS/Enterprise renewal at $287,644 in 2026/27 rising 5% a year to $349,633, and the record shows no benchmarking or alternatives (5-0 vote, July 14, 2026). Danbury, CT renewed OpenGov ($71,490.65) and Tyler MUNIS ($299,274.89) unanimously as sole-source because each vendor 'is the developer of proprietary systems' (Aug 5, 2026). In National City, CA a councilmember balked at a $250,000 Tyler budgeting module ('It is a $250,000'), the public questioned the sole-source, and the council demanded a white paper with precise terms and fees.
ideas.solution: Continuously ingest agenda packets from the big agenda platforms (Legistar, Granicus, CivicClerk, CivicPlus AgendaCenter) and use LLM extraction to build a structured contract table: vendor, product, price, term, escalator, termination clause, and normalized unit metrics (per capita, per seat, per officer, per camera). Anyone facing a renewal enters the vendor and product and gets a one-page brief within a day. It gives the comparable set, the median escalator, the clauses other governments got (price caps, termination for convenience, data-export rights) and a draft sole-source price-reasonableness paragraph the purchasing officer can attach to the staff report. Later: optional negotiation support on success fee.
ideas.why_now: Multi-year Tyler and other vendor contracts are coming up for renewal in 2026, and budgets are squeezed by federal cost shifts (SNAP admin share rising to 75% in October 2026) and grant uncertainty. Agenda packets are now machine-readable at scale. Cheap LLM extraction turns a decade of scattered PDFs into a price table, which was not economically possible before.
ideas.revenue_model: $495-1,500 per renewal brief; $3k/year unlimited briefs for a county; 15% of first-year savings for negotiated renewals. Secondary revenue: a quarterly 'what governments pay' index for councils and state associations of counties.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce item is not the data, it is a price-reasonableness determination. Sole-source is only defensible when the buyer can document that the price is reasonable, and none of these records shows one. The public packets already contain the answer, and every vendor claims pricing is confidential while its own contracts are posted in agenda PDFs. Evidence: Steuben County renewal, no alternatives documented (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9150000/new-york/steuben-county/finance-secures-fiveyear-renewal-pricing-for-munisenterprise-erp-committee-approves); Danbury sole-source renewals (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8951200/connecticut/fairfield/danbury-city/board-renews-opengov-and-tyler-munis-contracts-totaling-roughly-370000); National City council asking for the terms and fees (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9526083/california/san-diego-county/national-city/council-asks-city-manager-for-white-paper-after-tyler-technologies-budgeting-demo). Elko's five-year Axon extension at about $91,200 a year is another comparable data point (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog).
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape agenda packets from 300 mid-size jurisdictions in 2 states and extract about 500 contracts for 5 vendors. Publish a free 'What governments actually pay Tyler' leaderboard to earn inbound. Identify contracts expiring in 6-9 months from the term dates in old packets and email those finance directors a free sample brief. Sell the first 10 briefs at $495. Get 2 governments to attach the memo to a staff report as a proof point.

ideas.title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
ideas.one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
ideas.customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
ideas.problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
ideas.solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
ideas.why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
ideas.first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

ideas.title: Second-opinion technical review for city data center deals
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-fee package for small cities facing a data center: adversarial review of the developer's noise, water and power submissions, plus a term sheet built from the few community benefit agreements that exist.
ideas.customer: Planning directors, city managers and county administrators in jurisdictions under a data center moratorium or first inquiry, mostly populations of 5k-150k that cannot afford a big-firm consultant. They pay $8k-25k per package, and the cost can often be recovered from the applicant through an escrow for third-party review.
ideas.problem: Small governments are negotiating blind against developers' consultants. Broken Arrow, OK issued an RFQ for consultants to 'advise on environmental, water, noise, utilities and fiscal modeling' and needs recommendations by year-end 2026 or a moratorium extension. Fort Worth voted unanimously for a moratorium, Chicago introduced one in September 2026, and Lexington, KY paused approvals until at least Oct 31, 2026. NPR reports that deals such as the one in Boyce, Louisiana were negotiated under NDAs. The Federation of American Scientists found only eight executed community benefit agreements, only one fully executed and publicly posted (Lancaster, PA), and says 'best practices are not readily available'.
ideas.solution: A productized package. (1) An ordinance with fill-in standards: setbacks, dBA limits at the property line, closed-loop or reclaimed-water requirements, decommissioning bond, and utility-capacity verification. (2) A fiscal calculator comparing abatement to service and infrastructure costs, plus water/wastewater and power-interconnection checks. (3) A term-sheet library annotated from the known executed CBAs. (4) A retained on-call review of the developer's noise study, water plan and load forecast by contract engineers, with a plain-language memo the council can read in open session. Moratorium end dates are natural deadlines that pull purchases forward.
ideas.why_now: Data center siting became the top local land-use fight of 2026: Wixom MI, Denver, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Lexington, Broken Arrow and Chicago all acted this year, and more cities keep opening moratorium clocks. Developer NDAs are now a political issue, which pushes officials to buy independent review.
ideas.revenue_model: $8k-25k fixed fee per package; $2.5k/month retainer during active negotiation; per-review fee for developer-funded escrow; a subscription comparables database (abatement terms, water allocations, decommissioning bonds) for state municipal leagues.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Ordinance templates are free and cities can copy them; the scarce thing is an adversarial reader of the developer's technical submissions, because the city's only counterpart is the developer's own consultants under NDA. Applicant-funded escrow lets the city avoid a budget fight, so procurement is quick. Evidence: Broken Arrow's RFQ scope and year-end deadline (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9481196/oklahoma/tulsa-county/broken-arrow/city-council-meetings/city-forms-datacenter-study-committee-says-ordinance-moratorium-remains-in-place); the gap in best practices and only eight executed CBAs (https://fas.org/publication/data-center-community-benefit-agreements/); NDA-shrouded deals (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/27/nx-s1-5879528/data-center-nda-disclosure-louisiana); Fort Worth's unanimous moratorium (https://fortworthreport.org/2026/08/12/data-center-moratorium-takes-first-steps-after-fort-worth-city-councils-unanimous-vote/).
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a free comparison of the eight known CBAs and a one-page 'questions to ask a data center developer' for planning directors. Email 30 planning directors in cities with moratoria expiring in the next 6 months. Line up 2 retired utility or acoustic engineers as contract reviewers. Sell 2 fixed-fee review memos at $6k each, ideally funded by the applicant's escrow.

ideas.title: Vendor-neutral body-cam redaction bureau with fee pass-through
ideas.one_liner: A CJIS-cleared remote team that returns double-reviewed redacted police video priced per minute below the fee small cities already charge requesters, so the bureau funds itself.
ideas.customer: Small police departments and sheriff's offices (roughly 5-60 sworn officers) with records backlogs, and the city clerks and attorneys who carry the liability. They pay $0.40-0.60 per video minute plus a small monthly minimum.
ideas.problem: Small agencies do not have redaction staff. Elko, NV's police chief described about a year of catching up on redaction requests with no full-time redaction team and approved a five-year Axon extension of about $91,200 a year. White Salmon, WA has only two trained employees and set a $0.84-per-minute redaction fee (4-1 vote, April 15, 2026) while the chief said he 'cannot readily add a second-review step for all releases' because of limited trained staff and high request volume. A councilor dissented, arguing that sensitive footage such as juveniles needs more than one reviewer. Phoenix has nearly 40,000 pending public-records requests and raised commercial fees to pay for staff. AI-generated request floods (Somerset County, PA saw dozens a day) make it worse.
ideas.solution: A regional redaction bureau. Departments send only the clips requested (through share links from Axon, Motorola/WatchGuard, Getac and Wolfcom or others) and get back redacted video plus a redaction log within 5 business days. Automated face, plate and audio detection does the first pass. Then two trained human reviewers sign off, with a state-specific checklist (juveniles, victims, medical, informants). The bureau also sells 'backlog amnesty sprints' at a flat rate to clear a year-old queue. Vendor neutrality is the selling point, since Axon's automated redaction only helps agencies inside its ecosystem and still requires manual verification.
ideas.why_now: Body camera adoption is nearly universal after 2025-2026 contract cycles (Elko, Plainview, Crescent City, Carlsbad, Kasson approvals), public-records volume is up, and states are formalizing per-minute cost recovery. Councils are now adopting the fee schedules that make a pass-through model possible.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-minute fee ($0.40-0.60) billed to the agency, which recovers most or all of it from requesters at its own per-minute fee (White Salmon: $0.84); monthly minimum of $250; flat-rate backlog sprints of $5k-20k.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not blurring speed, it is a defensible second review on sensitive content, which small departments cannot staff. The fee schedule councils are adopting is derived from a cost-of-service study, so the department can pass the bureau's cost straight through; the bureau's margin lies between its price and the city's published fee. CJIS clearance and background checks form the moat that keeps generic video-AI startups out. Evidence: Elko's year-long backlog (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog); White Salmon's two trained employees, the $0.84/minute fee and the second-review dissent (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8492326/washington/klickitat-county/white-salmon/council-updates-public-records-policy-approves-084-per-minute-body-camera-redaction-fee-over-staff-objections); Phoenix's roughly 40,000 pending requests (https://www.kjzz.org/politics/2026-09-24/commercial-public-records-requests-prices-have-gone-up-in-phoenix-in-effort-to-hire-more-staff).
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state, such as Washington, with strong public-records laws and many small departments. Sign the CJIS security addendum with 2 agencies and have all reviewers fingerprint-cleared. Find 15 departments with a visible backlog in recent council minutes and offer a flat 'backlog amnesty sprint' on their first 500 minutes at $0.45/min. Turn the state's checklist into a review template and deliver the first 3 jobs within the month.

ideas.title: Two-Way Kasuhara Desk for Tiny Japanese Businesses
ideas.one_liner: A QR-and-LINE 'complaint lane' plus staff backup button that gives micro-businesses the customer-harassment policy, consultation channel and evidence log Japan now requires.
ideas.customer: Owners of Japanese businesses with 1-100 employees that face customers in person (izakaya, clinics, salons, cram schools, taxi and care operators, retail). They pay ¥2,980-9,800 per site per month. Resale channels are sharoushi (labor and social-insurance consultants) and SME insurance agents.
ideas.problem: From 1 Oct 2026 every Japanese employer with at least one employee must publish a policy against customer harassment ('kasuhara'), set up and publicize a consultation channel, and have response procedures. There is no phase-in. Most tiny firms have no HR function, no policy and no channel. Staff also hesitate to report incidents. Customers, for their part, now hesitate to voice legitimate complaints.
ideas.solution: (1) A QR code at the counter, on receipts and on LINE opens a structured, polite complaint form (what happened, photo, desired resolution). The owner gets a timestamped record, and abusive or threatening messages are flagged. (2) A 'need backup' button in LINE gives frontline staff an anonymous route to a partner sharoushi or counselor. That route is the required consultation channel. (3) A one-tap incident log that creates a dated evidence pack (notes, optional call-recording notice, response taken). (4) A policy, poster and work-rule addendum generator that meets the MHLW guideline. (5) A monthly 'compliance proof' PDF for the day the labor bureau asks.
ideas.why_now: The MHLW guideline was published on 26 Feb 2026 and the duty takes effect 1 Oct 2026, three days from today. Incumbent tooling targets call centers, such as SoftBank's SoftVoice AI voice-softener launched Feb 2026. Nothing is priced or packaged for a 5-person restaurant. The Oct 1 news cycle will also push owners to search for a fix.
ideas.revenue_model: ¥2,980/month per site (¥9,800 for 10+ staff), ¥30,000 optional setup for work-rule revision, and a 30% recurring rev-share to sharoushi and insurance agents who resell it. A later upsell is per-incident counselor escalation. Insurers may white-label it into SME liability packages.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The law has a hidden chilling effect on the customer side. In the Channel Corporation survey (497 customer-facing employees plus 514 consumers, June 2026), 52.3% of consumers who hit a store error 'let it pass' for fear of being labelled a harasser, and 65.2% wanted AI-mediated ways to raise issues. A product that gives customers a legitimate complaint lane defuses harassment at the source and doubles as the mandatory paper trail. Enforcement is guidance and then naming rather than fines, so buyers want the cheapest defensible record, not AI detection. Only under 10% of firms use technical measures. Evidence: KiteRa survey of 965 workers on 10-11 Sep 2026 found 61.3% with no policy, 68.3% with no publicized channel, 58.6% of firms with 100 or fewer employees with no channel at all, and 19.8% of workers harassed in the past year, of whom 74.9% hesitated to report (https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000130.000045846.html). Channel Corp found 51.7% with no measures at all (https://ecnomikata.com/ecnews/customerservice/51126/). Legal scope and enforcement: https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2026/singapore/customer-harassment-prevention-now-a-statutory-obligation-for-employers-in-japan. Incumbent focus on call centers: https://www.softbank.jp/en/sbnews/entry/20260219_01.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-3: Ship a free policy-and-poster generator plus a LINE Official Account to catch Oct 1 search traffic, and a landing page in Japanese. Days 4-14: Recruit 5-10 sharoushi (offer 30% recurring share and a white-label report) and 2 local shokokai chambers; sell 'compliance by Friday' to their existing clients. Build the QR complaint form with LINE Messaging API (no app needed) and manually route staff-backup messages to one partner counselor. Days 15-30: Sign 30-50 shops at ¥2,980 and collect 3 named case studies. Ask an SME insurance agency to pilot a bundled offer.

ideas.title: Unfreeze Desk for Indian UPI Merchants
ideas.one_liner: A court-ready dossier generator and fixed-fee advocate network that unfreezes shopkeepers' bank accounts after a scam victim's UPI money passes through them, with a freeze-continuity layer later.
ideas.customer: Small merchants, traders, fuel-station owners and freelancers in India whose current or savings accounts get frozen because a scam victim's money passed through their UPI QR. They pay per case (₹3,000-8,000) or a ₹199/month subscription. Chartered accountants and trader associations are the referral channel.
ideas.problem: Automated cyber-fraud freezes catch innocent recipients. One Faridabad scam of ₹4.43 crore led to more than 36,000 frozen accounts, mostly small merchants. A Mumbai shop owner was frozen over ₹826 and spent over a month trying to get access back. A retailer's ₹8.26 lakh current account was blocked over a single ₹1,000 UPI payment. Relief takes months, and working capital, payroll and supplier payments stall.
ideas.solution: Merchants upload the bank statement and freeze notice, and software extracts the flagged credit, payer VPA, invoices and merchant-vintage evidence. It then produces a bundle for the bank nodal officer and police investigating officer, and a draft writ petition citing the Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Rajasthan High Court rulings that a merchant cannot verify each UPI payer. Partner advocates file and appear at a fixed fee, and the tool tracks the case. Phase 2: a 'clean receipts' setup (order-ID dynamic QR, invoice per payment, a separate working-capital account) and an NBFC-funded bridge advance against the frozen balance.
ideas.why_now: The Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled in July 2026 that authorities cannot freeze a merchant's whole account for receiving a UPI payment from an accused, and other High Courts have said the same. That gives a template-able legal remedy where before it was ad hoc. The Faridabad freezes and the Home Ministry review put the problem in the news. UPI acceptance among tiny merchants keeps growing.
ideas.revenue_model: Fixed case fee of ₹3,000-8,000 (unfreeze package plus advocate), a ₹199/month 'Merchant Shield' subscription that keeps an evidence dossier updated, and referral fees from NBFC partners for frozen-balance bridge loans. Later B2B licensing to UPI QR aggregators and bank merchant-onboarding teams.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The merchant is not defrauded. The loss is working capital held hostage by a blunt automated tool that recovers almost nothing, so banks over-freeze. A Parliamentary Standing Committee found only ₹0.57 crore recovered out of ₹2,294.79 crore lost to cyber fraud in 2022, about 0.02%. So the freeze is structural false-positive management, not an anti-fraud problem, and the buyer is desperate on day one. Police in Faridabad said 'People come crying. Some had only ₹200 or ₹500 transferred to their accounts, yet the banks froze them.' Evidence: https://the420.in/faridabad-cyber-scam-upi-fraud-accounts-frozen-home-ministry/ and https://www.medianama.com/2026/07/223-merchants-bank-accounts-frozen-upi-payments-fraudsters-andhra-hc/.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-5: Build a WhatsApp intake bot and landing page in Hindi and English ('Account freeze ho gaya? 10 minute mein case file'). Sign 3 partner advocates in Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Hyderabad at a fixed split. Days 5-15: Template the dossier and petition from the three High Court rulings and have the advocates review it. Post explainer videos in Hindi and Gujarati on YouTube and Reels, and in trader WhatsApp and Telegram groups where frozen merchants already vent. Days 15-30: Close the first 20-30 paid cases, publish anonymized turnaround times, and approach two CA firms and one trader association for referrals. The design must keep filings with licensed advocates to avoid unauthorized-practice issues.

ideas.title: Deposit Gate That Kills Korean Bulk-Order Scams
ideas.one_liner: A KakaoTalk-native verify-and-deposit link that small Korean restaurants, bakeries and caterers send to any big or suspicious order, since scammers never pay a deposit and real customers do.
ideas.customer: Korean self-employed food, bakery, flower and catering owners who take phone or chat bulk orders. They pay ₩9,900/month plus a 1.5-2.5% take rate on deposits. Restaurant and bakery associations, POS vendors and card acquirers are distribution partners.
ideas.problem: The 'no-show scam' impersonates a government office, military unit, broadcaster or political party and places a large legitimate-looking order. The scammer then asks the owner to buy unrelated goods from a designated supplier, promising to pay for everything together. The owner pays the fake supplier and loses the money. It is 100% preventable by process, yet owners are alone on the phone and busy.
ideas.solution: The owner taps a Kakao chatbot or shortcut during the call. The caller receives a verify-and-deposit link: PASS phone identity, a claimed-organization check against official directories with call-back numbers, and a 10-30% deposit via KakaoPay or Toss. A tripwire flags any request to buy from a third-party supplier, which is the hallmark of stage two of the scheme. Scams die at the deposit step. Legitimate bulk buyers pay a small deposit, which also cuts ordinary no-shows.
ideas.why_now: H1 2025 losses were roughly 90% of the whole of 2024, with per-case damage up more than 50% year on year. Scammers keep widening the impersonations to entertainment agencies, broadcasters and political parties. Authorities' advice is already 'ask for a deposit', but nothing operationalizes it for a shop owner. KakaoPay and Toss make micro-deposit links trivial.
ideas.revenue_model: ₩9,900/month per shop, plus 1.5-2.5% of each deposit processed. B2B2C licensing to POS and reservation vendors, and fraud-loss underwriting data for card and insurance partners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The theft is not the food order, it is the redirected procurement in stage two, so a single rule ('never buy from a supplier the customer names') is nearly precision-perfect and a deposit is a perfect filter. Police-reported H1 2025 damage was ₩115.5 billion (1,155억 won) across 3,936 cases, about ₩29M per case (https://www.straightnews.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=311867 and https://www.ccmessage.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=121353). The two-stage method and the government's own advice to require deposits and reject out-of-scope purchases are described at https://www.viva100.com/article/20250623501489. The same article cites a Hyundai Research Institute estimate that ordinary no-shows cost hospitality ₩4.5 trillion a year, so the scam-defense wedge extends into a much larger deposit-booking market.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-7: Build a Kakao Channel bot that sends a hosted page with PASS auth, a deposit request via a payment gateway such as Toss Payments, and a scam-pattern checklist. Days 8-20: Offer free pilots to 50 shops via bakery, catering and restaurant owner Kakao open-chat groups and the local Food Service Association branch, with a scam-script sticker for the phone. Days 21-30: Convert the pilots that actually used it, publish a first 'blocked scam' tally, and approach one POS vendor and one card-acquirer with a co-branded offer.

ideas.title: Demumu With a Body: Paid Welfare-Check Responders
ideas.one_liner: Parent-paid check-in safety for Chinese-, Indian- and Korean-speaking students and migrants living alone abroad, where a missed check-in triggers a paid local door-knock instead of an email to someone 10,000 km away.
ideas.customer: Parents (in China, India, Korea) of students and young professionals living alone abroad, who pay about $6/month plus about $45 per dispatched welfare check. Universities' international offices are a secondary channel.
ideas.problem: The viral Chinese app 'Are You Dead?' (renamed Demumu) proves demand for solo-living safety, but its only action is an email alert to two emergency contacts. For migrants those contacts are usually parents or friends in another city or country who cannot physically check. China has more than 125 million one-person households, projected at 200 million by 2030. About two-thirds of solo dwellers are aged 20-59, i.e. young migrants rather than the elderly.
ideas.solution: A student-controlled check-in app (student chooses the circle, parents pay). After a missed check-in, the escalation is: push, SMS and call, then roommates and landlord, and finally a vetted local responder who does a door-knock with a photo-verified report and can escalate to the local non-emergency welfare-check line or emergency services. The responders are recruited from the same student and gig pool as China's 'companion economy' providers, in host cities such as Boston, London, Sydney and Toronto.
ideas.why_now: Demumu's rebrand and global launch in January 2026 put the format on top of app charts in China and among paid utilities in the West, so users now trust the idea. Anyone can clone the basic check-in app in a weekend, since it reportedly cost about ¥1,500 to build. The defensible layer is physical response, which the viral app doesn't have. A 50 billion yuan ($7.4B) Chinese 'companionship economy' shows that people pay for on-demand human presence.
ideas.revenue_model: $6/month parent subscription, plus $45 per dispatch or prepaid packs of two. Later, university international-office licensing and insurer partnerships (travel and student health plans).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the solo-liver. It is the anxious relative paying $30-60k a year in tuition, for whom $6/month is trivial. The viral product's critical gap is what happens after the alert. Evidence: Demumu reportedly cost about ¥1,500 ($210) to build, alerts two emergency contacts by email, most solo dwellers are 20-59, and there are 125 million one-person households (https://theconversation.com/are-you-dead-chinas-viral-app-reveals-a-complex-reality-of-solo-living-and-changing-social-ties-274536). It was the top paid app in China at 8 yuan and hit the top paid utilities in Australia (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/14/chinese-app-are-you-dead-to-change-name-after-surge-in-popularity and https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-15/are-you-dead-app-changes-name-demumu/106228484). Companion providers already earn 3,000-5,000 yuan/month and one hiking firm grew from under 10 to 370 workers (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/hiking-hotpot-lonely-consumers-china-031456787.html), so a responder supply pool exists.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-7: White-label a check-in flow (Twilio plus a simple app or LINE/WeChat mini-program) and write parent-facing Chinese copy. Recruit and vet 10 responders (graduate students) in 3 cities, with a code of conduct and background check. Days 8-20: Post on Xiaohongshu 'studying abroad' and 'parents of overseas students' and in WeChat parent groups, offering a free first month. Days 21-30: Convert 100 parent subscribers, run at least 3 real dispatches and publish the anonymized outcomes. Test privacy and consent wording with 20 students, because the student must opt in and control the circle. Assumption to test: parents' willingness to pay, and student acceptance.

ideas.title: Payday-Shaped Pix Automático Cadence for Low-Income Billers
ideas.one_liner: A layer on top of Brazilian gateways that designs the recurring-debit cadence (weekly, biweekly, payday-aligned) and consent options at enrollment, so small billers stop losing all-or-nothing monthly debits.
ideas.customer: Small Brazilian businesses billing low-income or irregular-income payers on a recurring basis: neighborhood ISPs, small gyms, neighborhood schools, discount-card clinics, motorbike-rental fleets for delivery couriers (to validate first), and insurance or consórcio sellers. They pay 10-15% of incremental collected revenue.
ideas.problem: Pix Automático collects the full amount or nothing, with no partial debits. Retries are limited to 3 in 7 days and only if the payer consented. The payer can cancel or edit the mandate up to the eve of the debit, and the mandate cannot change frequency or amount ceiling after authorization. Meanwhile 83.9 million Brazilians were in negative credit standing in August 2026, a record. Monthly lump debits collide with irregular income, and small merchants still chase payers by hand every month.
ideas.solution: At enrollment, quote cadence from the payer's income rhythm (weekly for app-paid couriers and informal workers, biweekly for 'vale' and salary splits, monthly for salaried payers) and create the correct mandate with retries-consent and, optionally, credit-line consent. A WhatsApp 'pre-debit rescue' 48-72 hours before each charge lets the payer confirm, move the date to just after payday, pause, or split into a new mandate, instead of silently cancelling in the bank app. Built as an API layer over a gateway that already exposes the retry policy, such as Asaas. Reports per merchant show debit success rate, cancellation reasons and recovered revenue.
ideas.why_now: Pix Automático launched in June 2025 and adoption is compounding. Companies had to be able to offer it from 1 Jan 2026, and it is far cheaper than cards and has no chargebacks. About 60% of low-income Brazilians lack credit cards, so account-debit is the only recurring rail for that segment. Most tooling so far is generic dunning, not cadence design.
ideas.revenue_model: Performance-based: 10-15% of incremental collected revenue versus the merchant's baseline, or a flat R$149/month for merchants who prefer subscription. Later a per-debit micro-fee and a marketplace of payer-side 'payday buffers'.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The frequency is locked at authorization, so cadence is an irreversible, high-leverage decision at signup, and nobody optimizes it. Because partial collection is not allowed, the only way to fit a low-income payer's cashflow is to change the shape of the debits, not to chase them afterwards. Evidence: PagBrasil reports +182% transactions and +181% new users quarter over quarter from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026, and a coffee subscriber cut churn 25.2% and cost 50% versus cards (https://www.pagbrasil.com/blog/recurring-payments/automatic-pix-2026/). Serasa reported 83.9 million negativados in August 2026 (https://www.shipay.com.br/inadimplencia-no-brasil-como-melhorar-cobrancas/). Rules on no partials, 3 retries in 7 days and cancellation until the day before are at https://celcoin.com.br/articles/vale-a-pena-pix-automatico/ and https://docs.asaas.com/docs/faq-2. The mandate 'cannot change the frequency' and 60% of low-income Brazilians lack cards (https://www.pymnts.com/news/payments-innovation/2025/pix-automatico-debut-opens-brazils-recurring-payments-market-to-millions/). Small billers describe the monthly grind: 'Todo mês alguém precisa lembrar o cliente, mandar mensagem, enviar chave Pix, cobrar boleto atrasado' (https://www.alfadenegocios.com.br/2026/08/pix-automatico-para-pequenos-negocios.html).
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1-3: Confirm in the BCB spec which recurrence periodicities are permitted (weekly and biweekly are assumed, not yet verified) and the per-debit fee, since more frequent debits cost more per charge. Fall back to monthly with payday-aligned dates plus split mandates if not. Days 4-15: Build a thin layer over the Asaas API and a WhatsApp pre-debit rescue flow. Recruit 10 merchants from a single vertical, ideally neighborhood ISPs or courier motorbike-rental fleets, through their ERP user groups and Facebook groups. Days 16-30: Run a split test (monthly vs payday-aligned vs weekly) on new enrollments, report debit success and cancellations, and sign the first 3-5 performance-fee contracts.

ideas.title: Blank-First Microplastics: Clean Kits and Data Forensics
ideas.one_liner: Sell certified low-shed sampling kits, blank/spike proficiency samples, and legacy-data re-analysis to microplastics labs whose glove-contaminated numbers are now in doubt.
ideas.customer: Environmental testing labs pursuing state microplastics accreditation, public water utilities that must test and report, university microplastics groups, and beverage/bottled-water QA labs. Litigation and NGO teams that need defensible numbers are a secondary buyer.
ideas.problem: Routine nitrile and latex gloves shed stearate particles that read as microplastics, adding about 2,000 false-positive signals per mm² in University of Michigan tests. Labs are 'searching for the needle in the haystack' and are unsure how much of their existing data is contaminated. Labs cannot reliably tell real microplastics from consumable-derived artifacts.
ideas.solution: 1) 'Blank-first' kits with characterized cleanroom gloves, pre-cleaned filters, slides and foil, plus lot-level FTIR/Raman shed certificates. 2) Blind spiked reference samples for inter-lab proficiency checks. 3) A data-forensics service that re-screens a lab's archived spectra and micrographs for stearate signatures, using the published discrimination approach. 4) A public 'shed scoreboard' of glove and consumable brands to build trust and inbound leads.
ideas.why_now: The Michigan glove-artifact paper appeared in RSC Analytical Methods in 2026, and it says affected datasets can potentially be recovered. California's drinking-water microplastics program (SB 1422) has adopted IR and Raman methods and plans four years of testing and reporting. Its 22-lab intercomparison flagged accuracy and precision as needing improvement, so lab demand for defensible negatives is rising just as the artifact becomes public.
ideas.revenue_model: Consumable kits at roughly $300-1,000 per kit with recurring lot replenishment. Proficiency-sample subscriptions at roughly $2-5k per lab per year. Fixed-price legacy-data re-analysis packages at roughly $5-25k, and certification-lot fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a measurement crisis the money is in negative controls, not in a better detector. The demand evidence is the University of Michigan finding of ~2,000 false positives/mm² from ordinary gloves and 'thousands of times higher than expected' counts (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/03/260329222938.htm). California's inter-laboratory study also says methods need better accuracy and precision through training and refinement (https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/microplastics.html). Every lab that ever wore nitrile gloves has a reason to buy reassurance, and the researchers themselves say old datasets can be salvaged, which creates a service market.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy about 10 glove brands, filters and slides, and run shed tests through a university core-facility FTIR or Raman instrument to produce a public shed scoreboard. Write to the paper's authors and about 30 accredited environmental labs and utility QA managers. Sell the first 10 pilot kits at cost-plus and offer 2-3 discounted forensic re-analyses in exchange for case studies.

ideas.title: Pre-Confirmation Screwworm Risk Feed for Cattle Markets
ideas.one_liner: A county-level early-warning feed that fuses news, vet reports, weather and zone announcements to give cattle buyers, auction barns and insurers days or weeks of lead time over official lab confirmation.
ideas.customer: Auction markets and sale barns, feedlots and stocker buyers, livestock lenders and insurers, and cattle-futures or ag-commodity desks. Ranchers and vet clinics are a low-price tier.
ideas.problem: New World screwworm has reached Texas and New Mexico. The UC San Diego team building a tracker says official reporting lags: 'Lab confirmation can take days or weeks.' Cattle prices, hauling rules and purchase decisions move on rumor and news before confirmation. Producers have no single source for zone status and their own exposure.
ideas.solution: A subscription feed that scores county-level risk from public and semi-public signals: state and APHIS zone announcements, extension and vet-clinic posts, local news, trap and case reports, and fly-friendly temperature and humidity. It sends SMS or email alerts and a plain-language 'movement readiness' checklist for each zone. Users can submit their own sightings, which improves the model. Sold in tiers from a $99/month producer plan to trading-desk contracts.
ideas.why_now: The screwworm reached the US Southwest in 2026, and APHIS newsroom items on 18 and 21 September 2026 show Texas releasing infested zones. The academic dashboard is a research tool, not a commercial product, and the sterile-fly response is slow to scale, so risk and compliance uncertainty will last through at least one fly season.
ideas.revenue_model: Producer and barn subscriptions at $99-500/month, insurer, lender and buyer contracts at $2-10k/month, and enterprise API fees for commodity desks.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The academic value of the dashboard is the reporting lag itself: the UC San Diego team added media reports because 'lab confirmation can take days or weeks' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260914102439.htm). The paying customer is anyone whose money moves on news before USDA confirms, meaning buyers, hedgers and insurers, not the county health officials the tool was built for. The lag is the product. Recent APHIS announcements show zone status is changing week to week (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news).
ideas.first_30_days: Build a scraper and manual-curation pipeline over APHIS and Texas Animal Health Commission announcements, extension and vet feeds, and local news, plus a weather-based fly-activity index. Publish a free weekly map to gather emails. Pitch 10 sale barns and 3 commodity or insurer desks a paid pilot and sell the first 5 at a founding discount. Contact the UC San Diego team about a data and methods collaboration. Note that the APHIS screwworm page consulted in this session still said the pest was absent from the US, so confirm current case status before launch.

ideas.title: Rare Blood Group Assay Foundry
ideas.one_liner: Turn each newly recognized blood-group gene into research-use genotyping controls and panels for reference labs, starting with the MAL deletions that define AnWj-negative blood.
ideas.customer: Immunohematology reference labs, rare-donor programs and blood centers. Blood-group genotyping platform vendors that want to add content are a second buyer.
ideas.problem: AnWj-negative patients, over 99.9% of people are AnWj-positive, can form antibodies against AnWj and risk serious transfusion reactions from ordinary units, and compatible donors are 'extraordinarily difficult' to find. Antibody testing finds the patients but cannot identify rare genetic carriers or donors. Volumes are too small for large diagnostics companies to prioritize.
ideas.solution: A small molecular-biology team designs, validates and sells RUO kits: synthetic positive-control DNA for the published MAL deletions, primer and probe sets, and a small validation panel. It then repeats the process for each new ISBT system or rare antigen as the genes are published. It also licenses content to genotyping platform vendors and offers a sample-testing service for rare-donor registries.
ideas.why_now: MAL was formally recognized as ISBT blood group system 047 in 2026, and the authors say genotyping tests 'can potentially be incorporated into existing blood group genotyping systems.' Nobody has yet turned the finding into a commercial assay. Cheap gene synthesis and long-read or targeted sequencing make a low-volume, high-value control kit practical for a small team.
ideas.revenue_model: RUO control and primer kits at roughly $500-2,000 each, per-sample testing fees for registries, and content-licensing or royalty deals with platform vendors. Later, a CLIA or LDT lab service.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every new blood-group gene discovery creates a diagnostic gap that big vendors ignore because volume is tiny, and the 47th ISBT system was only just recognized. The NHS Blood and Transplant discovery took nearly 20 years and states that serological testing 'cannot identify rare genetic cases without genetic sequencing' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260918024828.htm; Blood 2024, DOI 10.1182/blood.2024025099). A repeatable foundry that converts each new ISBT gene into a control kit captures a stream of these gaps. Rare-donor matching is a high-willingness-to-pay niche because a single unmatched patient can cost a hospital far more than a kit.
ideas.first_30_days: Design gBlock-style synthetic controls for the MAL deletion alleles reported in the Blood paper and validate them on public or donated DNA. Contact the NHS Blood and Transplant IBGRL, the American Rare Donor Program and 5-10 US and EU reference labs to trial the RUO kit. Line up a second gene from the recent ISBT additions. Pitch two platform vendors on a content deal.

ideas.title: Hard-Alloy Print Recipes via Sample-Efficient AI Campaigns
ideas.one_liner: Sell validated 3D-print parameter recipes and 40-build AI-guided optimization campaigns so ordinary mid-power metal printers can make alloys that normally need rare high-power machines.
ideas.customer: Metal additive-manufacturing job shops and small rocket, space and defense suppliers with 400-500 W class printers. University AM labs are a secondary buyer.
ideas.problem: GRCop-42, a copper-chromium-niobium rocket-engine alloy, is hard and costly to print. It typically needs high laser power, and about 90% of commercial printers cannot handle it. Every failed build wastes powder and machine time, and shops cannot afford months of trial and error.
ideas.solution: A recipe library of machine-specific, validated parameter sets and build reports, sold per alloy and per machine model. It comes with a paid 'campaign' service that uses Bayesian or active-learning search to find working settings in about 40 builds from a few failed starting points. Customer builds feed back into the shared library.
ideas.why_now: Washington State University's team used AI to search over 100 million candidate settings, started from 37 failed experiments, and found 6 successful settings in 40 experiments over 3 months, including a first successful print at a record-low 500 W. The work won an Innovative Deployed Application Award, and active-learning frameworks for science are appearing on arXiv (for example arXiv:2609.31197). The method is proven and unlicensed to shops.
ideas.revenue_model: Recipe licenses at roughly $5-30k per alloy-machine pair, campaign fees of roughly $20-60k, and an annual recipe-library subscription for shops.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The product is not the alloy but the experiment budget. The WSU study says 90% of commercial printers cannot print GRCop-42 and that success required 'a very challenging case for AI' with rare successes, and the lead author says they are 'essentially democratizing the printing' of the alloy (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/08/260827010504.htm). Selling failure-avoidance to shops that cannot afford 37 failed builds is a service business, not a materials business.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact the WSU authors and WSU's commercialization office about licensing the method. Recruit 2-3 job shops with 400-500 W machines and quote a fixed-price GRCop-42 campaign, with the shop supplying powder and machine time. Pre-sell the first recipe pack to rocket and space startups. Run the first campaign in month 2 and publish a build-report case study.

ideas.title: Skin-Tone-Verified SpO2 Validation Cooperative
ideas.one_liner: Build the 10x-larger, objectively skin-tone-measured, arterial-blood-paired dataset that pulse-oximeter and wearable makers need, and sell access, bias reports and validation studies.
ideas.customer: Pulse-oximeter and wearable OEMs and startups, plus hospital purchasing groups that want independent bias reports before buying devices.
ideas.problem: Current pulse oximeters tend to overestimate arterial saturation in darkly pigmented patients, so low oxygen can go undetected. A new arXiv correction method works on 98 patients from the public OpenOximetry Repository but the authors say a cohort roughly ten times larger is needed for significance. The 2013 FDA 510(k) guidance asks for only 'at least 2 darkly pigmented subjects or 15% of your subject pool' and says nothing of objective pigmentation measures.
ideas.solution: Recruit a diverse cohort and characterize each participant with a skin reflectance spectrometer to get melanin fraction. Run induced-hypoxia studies with paired arterial samples through partner university hypoxia labs. License the de-identified dataset and calibration models to OEMs, and offer per-device bias validation and a public 'bias report card' for hospital buyers.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 arXiv paper by Blaney, Fantini, Koomson and colleagues shows a melanin-aware correction that cut error from +2.8 to +0.1 percentage points per unit melanin fraction, but it is data-limited. Wearable SpO2 features are now mainstream, and regulators and buyers are asking for skin-tone-diverse evidence. I could not verify in this session the status of the January 2025 FDA draft guidance, so confirm it before pitching.
ideas.revenue_model: Dataset licenses of roughly $50-250k, per-device validation studies of $100-400k, and annual bias-report subscriptions for hospital groups and OEMs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is data, not algorithms. The arXiv paper says current oximeters 'overestimate arterial saturation in darkly pigmented patients', its correction relies on per-patient skin-tone measurement, and 'a cohort roughly ten times larger is needed' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30122). The current FDA 510(k) guidance sets a low bar of 2 darkly pigmented subjects or 15% of the pool (https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/pulse-oximeters-premarket-notification-submissions-510ks-guidance-industry-and-food-and-drug). Whoever owns the largest objectively measured dataset sets the de facto standard, and every OEM has to buy or replicate it.
ideas.first_30_days: Email the arXiv authors and OpenOximetry contributors about their data needs. Sign a partner hypoxia lab and an IRB pathway, and design a 30-50 participant pilot. Pre-sell the pilot dataset to 3 wearable or oximeter startups through LOIs. Prototype a spectrometer-based melanin measurement protocol and publish a pre-registered study plan.

ideas.title: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Eligibility and Prior-Auth Navigator
ideas.one_liner: A 2-minute eligibility check and clinician-ready prior-auth packet for the $50/month Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, sold to caregivers, independent pharmacies and primary-care offices before the window closes in December 2027.
ideas.customer: Two payers. (a) Gen X adult children (45-58, household income often above $100K) who manage a Medicare-age parent's medications and pay $29 per packet. (b) Independent pharmacies and small primary-care practices that pay $79/month to stop fielding the same eligibility and prior-auth questions by phone.
ideas.problem: Medicare started an 18-month GLP-1 Bridge on July 1, 2026. It costs $50/month for Wegovy, Zepbound or Foundayo, but eligibility is a maze. It needs a BMI of 35 or more, or BMI 30+ with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, uncontrolled hypertension or stage 3a+ kidney disease, or BMI 27+ with pre-diabetes, prior heart attack or stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease. Type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea and MASH disqualify you. So does having filled any GLP-1 under Part D in 2026. Prior authorization is required. Roughly 3.8M Part D enrollees qualify and about 5.9M are locked out, so sicker patients are routed to Part D copays of $200-600+ a month. One 68-year-old retired professor with BMI 42, a quadruple bypass and sleep apnea told KFF Health News: 'I'm obese, morbidly obese, BMI 42... And yet I can't get it.'
ideas.solution: A plain-language quiz built from the published Bridge criteria. It flags the traps, such as a 2026 Part D GLP-1 fill or a sleep apnea diagnosis. It outputs one of three routes: Bridge, Part D with an expected copay, or a manufacturer cash price (TrumpRx lists $149-$299/month). It then generates a prior-authorization documentation checklist and cover letter for the prescriber (BMI evidence, comorbidity codes, exclusion attestation). Pharmacies and practices get a white-label link and a shared queue of who is waiting on what. It stays plan-neutral: no plan enrollment and no commissions from carriers, which keeps it outside Medicare marketing rules (confirm with counsel).
ideas.why_now: The Bridge began July 1, 2026 and ends December 2027, so the demand window is 15 months and open enrollment starts October 15, about 3 weeks from now. CMS is also ending the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026. That subsidy had cut average premiums by $26 in 2025 and $16 in 2026, and about 24.9M people are in stand-alone drug plans that may face bigger 2027 increases. Oral options (Wegovy pill approved December 2025, Foundayo approved April 2026) widen the eligible pool. Nobody has built a workflow product for a program this new and this temporary.
ideas.revenue_model: $29 one-time per beneficiary packet (caregiver-paid). $79/month per independent pharmacy or clinic for white-label link, queue and templates. Optional $15 per completed PA-submission assist. Sunset risk is real, so design the engine to carry over to whatever CMS replaces the Bridge with (KFF flags a coming BALANCE model).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The eligibility rules create a paradox where the sicker you are, the more you pay. Sleep apnea or diabetes disqualifies patients from the $50 Bridge and pushes them into $200-600+ Part D copays, which can exceed manufacturer cash prices ($199 Wegovy pen, $299 Zepbound on TrumpRx). That gap creates demand for a neutral router rather than another telehealth prescriber. Evidence: KFF's Bridge criteria, cost and start/end dates https://www.kff.org/medicare/nearly-four-million-medicare-beneficiaries-met-the-eligibility-criteria-in-2023-for-the-medicare-glp-1-bridge/ ; the excluded-patient quote, 5.9M figure and Part D copay range https://kffhealthnews.org/aging/medicare-glp1-bridge-weight-loss-drugs-coverage-exceptions-cost-access/ ; premium-subsidy end and 24.9M stand-alone enrollees https://www.kff.org/quick-insights/cmss-decision-to-end-temporary-subsidies-to-medicares-stand-alone-drug-plans-could-mean-larger-premium-increases-for-some-beneficiaries-next-year/ ; cash prices https://trumprx.gov/ . To verify: whether Medicare beneficiaries can actually use cash-price channels, and how those purchases interact with Part D cap accounting. One fetched source (Wikipedia) implies TrumpRx has Medicare-specific pricing, which conflicts with the site's consumer prices.
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: turn the KFF criteria into a quiz and publish 'Do I qualify for the $50 Medicare GLP-1 Bridge?' pages timed to the October 15 open-enrollment spike. Week 2: post in Medicare and caregiver communities and pitch 10 independent pharmacies (NCPA-style networks) on a free white-label link. Week 3: get one primary-care practice to review the PA cover-letter template for clinical accuracy. Week 4: charge $29 for the packet. Target 100 paid packets and 5 pharmacies on $79/month. Keep it free of plan recommendations until compliance is reviewed.

ideas.title: Betting Profit-and-Loss Statements for Credit Unions
ideas.one_liner: Turn a member's bank ACH data into an 'investment-style' betting P&L (what they recovered per dollar deposited) and optional spending guardrails, licensed per member to credit unions and neobanks.
ideas.customer: Community banks, credit unions with young or college-town memberships, and neobanks, paying $0.25-0.60 per member per month. A free consumer version targets Gen Z bettors and their worried parents or partners.
ideas.problem: Online betting and prediction-market use is surging among the young. In June-July 2026 first-time users were about 3x January levels. Gen Z and Millennials were 88% of activity (Gen Z 48%). Bettors recovered under 75 cents per dollar sent to platforms. 23% of sports bettors bet daily and 34% weekly. Households that bet had a median deposit balance of only 59% of non-bettors'. Most of these users do not think of themselves as gamblers: 20% of respondents call sports betting a type of investment, Gen Z is about twice as likely to, and buying prediction-market event contracts is more likely to be called an investment than sports betting is.
ideas.solution: A detector that classifies ACH and card flows to sportsbooks, sweepstakes casinos and event-contract exchanges, using a maintained list of originator and descriptor names. It produces a plain 'Your realized return: -27%' statement in the vocabulary bettors already use (returns, cost basis), with a monthly summary and opt-in deposit caps or a cooling-off freeze. A parent, partner or co-guardian mode makes it useful for Gen Z members who live at home. The consumer version is a free upload-your-statement tool that generates a shareable 'what's your recovery ratio' card, which doubles as the top of the funnel for credit-union licenses.
ideas.why_now: Prediction markets went mainstream in 2026 and the FIFA World Cup drove the June-July spike. Football season, which overlaps other major leagues, starts a new peak now, and first-time users grew 22% YoY in the 2025 football season. Regulators and financial institutions are still working out how to treat event contracts. Under BofA's own framing they sit in a gray zone between entertainment and investing.
ideas.revenue_model: B2B: $2-5K/month pilot fees, then $0.25-0.60 per member per month. B2C: free P&L tool, $4.99/month for caps and alerts, and paid family co-guardian seats. Possible later add-on: aggregate, anonymized risk analytics for lenders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Self-serve gambling blocks fail because bettors do not classify themselves as gamblers, so a harm-reduction message framed as 'gambling addiction' gets ignored, while a return-on-investment statement speaks their mental model. BofA identified betting activity purely from ACH flows, which shows any bank can build the same detection. Working hypothesis, not verified because my search budget ran out: card merchant-category-code blocks used by many banks probably miss ACH-funded prediction-market deposits. Validate with two or three credit-union risk teams before building. Evidence: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/online-betting-platforms.html and its full PDF https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/online-betting-platforms.pdf (3x first-timers, recovery under 75 cents, 88% Gen Z plus Millennials, 20% see betting as investing, 59% median balance).
ideas.first_30_days: Week 1: compile a list of ACH originator and descriptor names for major sportsbooks, sweepstakes casinos and event-contract exchanges, and ship a client-side upload-a-CSV P&L calculator with a shareable result card. Week 2: seed it in Gen Z finance and sports-betting subreddits and Discords to collect real recovery-ratio numbers. Week 3: cold-email 30 credit unions near universities and military bases (member-financial-wellness and CUSO contacts) with the anonymized ratio data. Week 4: sign one or two paid pilots at $2-5K/month. Legal review of state gambling-related messaging rules is required before launch.

ideas.title: Half-Plate GLP-1 Menus for Independent Restaurants
ideas.one_liner: A menu-engineering kit that converts an independent restaurant's existing dishes into protein-first half-plates priced at about 65-75% of the full plate, to capture GLP-1 households that eat out smaller but still eat out.
ideas.customer: Independent and regional restaurants (10-60 seats, $1-4M revenue) in metros with a high share of higher-income Gen X and Boomer diners, paying $499 setup plus $99-149/month.
ideas.problem: Circana estimates 23% of US households now include a GLP-1 user and that these users will account for about 35% of food and beverage sales by 2030. Those households cut traditional retail food and beverage purchases, especially high-carb, high-sugar, refrigerated and frozen items, and shift toward protein, fiber, fresh produce and restaurant spending, yet they still outspend non-users. Big chains are chasing this, but independents have no menu-engineering staff. If they simply shrink portions at the same price, GLP-1 customers feel ripped off. If they shrink and cut the price proportionally, margins collapse.
ideas.solution: For each restaurant, a done-for-you overlay: 4-6 existing dishes re-specified as half-plates with protein grams, plate-cost and margin tables, pricing at 65-75% of full price to protect gross margin per cover, a small-plate 'protein first' section, and a nausea-friendly option (low-fat, low-volume). Deliverables include a printable menu insert, a QR page, POS/online-ordering item entries (Toast, Square, Clover) and simple local marketing via medspas, GLP-1 telehealth clinics and pharmacies that hand out a 'restaurants near you that fit your plan' card. Protein numbers come from recipe-level calculations, not vague 'healthy' badges.
ideas.why_now: GLP-1 adoption is at household scale (Circana, November 2025), and oral versions (Wegovy pill December 2025, Foundayo April 2026) plus cash prices as low as $149-$299/month on TrumpRx.gov are pulling in more users. Novo Nordisk is cutting list prices to $675/month in January 2027. Meanwhile restaurant spending is recovering, with independents beating national chains and Gen Z leading (BofA, August 2026), so independent owners are looking for a differentiator national brands cannot copy quickly.
ideas.revenue_model: $499 one-time setup, $99-149/month for menu updates, QR/landing page and local partnership marketing. Optional performance share (for example, $1 per redeemed 'plan card'). Later: bulk licensing to regional chains and food-service distributors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The obvious read is 'GLP-1 kills food demand'. The data says something different: users cut retail food but restaurant spending rises and total spend still exceeds non-users, so the demand shifts channel and portion size rather than disappearing. The winner is margin engineering (a half-plate that keeps dollars per cover), not a health-halo badge. Evidence: Circana (Nov 18, 2025) https://www.circana.com/post/glp-1-medication-users-to-represent-35-percent-of-u-s-food-and-beverage-sales-by-2030 and https://www.circana.com/insights-hub/glp-1s-consumer-behavior (23% of households, 35% by 2030, restaurants up, retail food down, users skew Gen X with income over $100K). Independents outperform chains: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/restaurants-and-discretionary-spending.html . Caveat: the Circana pages I could read did not give the size of the restaurant-spend lift, so validate it with a few owners' POS data.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro. Walk in on 20 independent restaurants with a one-page free audit of their own top 5 dishes (protein grams, half-plate cost and price). Convert 5-8 into paid setups. In parallel, sign 2-3 medspas or pharmacies to hand out the plan card and track redemptions to build a case study. Target: 5 paying restaurants and one measurable uplift story (covers or check average on half-plates) by day 30.

ideas.title: Rent Ledger for Adult Kids Living at Home
ideas.one_liner: A simple lease, payment and credit-reporting layer that lets parents charge their adult children rent, build the kids' credit history, and quietly bank the money as a down-payment fund.
ideas.customer: Parents (Gen X and Boomers) with adult children aged 22-30 living at home, paying $12/month per household. Secondary revenue from mortgage lenders and first-time-buyer programs.
ideas.problem: Nearly half (49%) of US adults under 30 lived with parents in 2025, up 12 percentage points from 2019 (Federal Reserve SHED). Only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or a paid-off card, and the Fed reports 16% of adults use buy-now-pay-later, with 11% of users hit by overdraft fees from missed payments. Lender-side data shows BNPL is spreading into groceries (a LendingTree survey reported nearly a quarter of BNPL users financed groceries, up from 14%; 41% reported a late payment). These young adults are paying for hobbies, subscriptions and installment plans while accruing no rent history at all, since informal family housing builds no credit and no savings discipline.
ideas.solution: An app that produces a simple parent-child lease, collects a modest monthly 'rent' by ACH, reports on-time payments to the credit bureaus through an established rent-reporting partner (do not become a furnisher), and lets the parent choose to escrow the money in a labeled account toward a future down payment or move-out fund. It gives the kid a monthly statement and a BNPL and subscription view so obligations don't collide with rent day. It includes parent-side documentation of the rent for tax purposes (tax treatment is a gray area, so it needs CPA-reviewed templates).
ideas.why_now: The 12-point jump in under-30s living at home is now structural, not a pandemic blip. Rent reporting has been mainstreamed by consumer fintechs and by underwriting systems that count rental payment history, and BNPL late payments are rising, which raises the value of a credibility-building habit. Housing costs make first-time down payments the main goal for these households.
ideas.revenue_model: $12/month per household (parent pays), $5/month optional kid add-on for credit-builder features. Referral fees from mortgage lenders and down-payment-assistance programs when the kid buys. Later: employer benefit channel for parents.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Parents are the largest unpriced landlord class in the US, and they already hold the leverage the market lacks: the kid will pay them and will not skip. The product isn't a rent app, it is a behavioral bridge that converts a free-rent arrangement into credit history plus parent-held savings. Evidence: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm (49% of under-30s living with parents, +12 points since 2019; 63% cover $400; 16% BNPL, 11% overdraft fees) and BNPL grocery and late-payment figures via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buy_now,_pay_later (summarizing LendingTree). Assumptions to validate first: that bureaus and lenders will accept rent reported for a parent-landlord and how underwriting treats it, and that parents want to charge rent and save it. I found no survey on either.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 20 parents in local parenting and finance Facebook groups. Test a landing page and a $12/month waitlist. Run a concierge pilot with 10 families: a lease template, ACH collection, an existing rent-reporting partner and a shared spreadsheet. Confirm with a mortgage broker whether reported parent-landlord rent helps underwriting. Target 15 paying families and one lender-partner conversation.

ideas.title: Second-Opinion Price Check for Vet Estimates
ideas.one_liner: Upload a photo of a vet estimate and get a line-by-line price benchmark and a list of questions to ask your vet within 24 hours, from vet-tech reviewers, for $19-29.
ideas.customer: Pet owners facing $500+ estimates (about 95M US households own pets), plus pet insurers and employers as a later benefit channel and independent clinics as a fair-price badge buyer.
ideas.problem: Vet services inflation ran 5.5% YoY in April 2026, and household spending at vets rose almost 4x as fast as spending on pet food and treats (about 1%). BofA Global Research says veterinary pricing is rising faster than wages, so many households delay wellness visits, dentistry and diagnostics. 25-30% of US veterinary practices, and roughly 75% of specialty clinics, are now owned by corporations or private equity (AVMA 2024, cited by BofA), which can erode competition. Pet insurance uptake stays low, and younger and lower-income households are pulling back on pet spending. When an owner is holding an estimate for a sick animal, there is no neutral benchmark.
ideas.solution: A mobile-first upload flow. OCR reads the estimate, and licensed vet techs (not diagnosing, just reviewing) compare each line item to regional price ranges, flag bundled or optional items, note which items are typically deferrable versus urgent, and give a short script of questions for the clinic. Every review adds anonymized line-item prices to a growing regional price database, which becomes the moat. Later features are a 'fair-price verified' badge for independent clinics and a payment-plan and generic-drug price check.
ideas.why_now: The data now shows a sharp split: sticker prices climb while pet food and store spending stalls, meaning owners are squeezed specifically at the vet. Private-equity consolidation is a live news story, and owners can share estimate photos easily. Pet-insurance carriers face rising claim costs and have an incentive to fund price transparency.
ideas.revenue_model: $19-29 per review, $9/month for unlimited pet-family plan, B2B licenses to insurers and employers ($1-3 per covered pet per month), and clinic subscriptions for verified fair-price badges ($99-199/month per clinic).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The pain is not that pet care costs money, it is information asymmetry at the moment of an estimate, and the same dynamic is what made medical-bill advocacy a business for humans. Vet inflation is running roughly 4x pet-food spending growth, and owners are already responding by deferring care rather than shopping around, so the demand is for a fast, trusted benchmark, not another directory. Evidence: BofA Institute, 'The price of pet parenting has gone off leash,' 18 May 2026 https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/pet-ownership-costs.html and full PDF https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/pet-ownership-costs.pdf (vet inflation 5.5% YoY, vet spending growth about 4x pet-store, 25-30% of practices corporate or PE owned, 95M pet households, $158B spend, deferred care). Legal caveat: state veterinary practice acts restrict diagnosing without a client-patient relationship, so reviewers must stay in price and question-generation territory.
ideas.first_30_days: Hire two contract vet techs at an hourly rate. Launch a landing page and post in owner communities and Reddit pet-cost threads with 'send me your estimate and I'll benchmark it free' to collect the first 100 estimates. Build the price table by hand in a spreadsheet, then charge $19 from review number 30. Approach one pet-insurance MGA or employer-benefit broker with the first regional benchmark chart. Target 100 reviews and 30 paid by day 30.

ideas.title: Fractional Licensed Qualifier for Trade-Business Buyers
ideas.one_liner: Rent a vetted master-licensed professional as the bona fide qualifying officer, so first-time buyers of HVAC, plumbing, electrical and engineering firms can get financed and keep the license alive after the seller leaves.
ideas.customer: First-time acquirers (search funders, SBA-financed individual buyers, independent sponsors, small holdcos) of licensed-trade companies with $1-15M revenue. The buyer pays monthly. SBA lenders and business brokers are the referral channel.
ideas.problem: In licensed trades the license and credentials are the real asset, and they walk out the door with the seller at closing. Buyers without a license get rejected by banks, and a replacement certification takes 6-12 months. Search-fund and ETA (entrepreneurship through acquisition) volume is at record levels, so more non-credentialed buyers are chasing these businesses.
ideas.solution: A bench of retired or semi-retired license holders (master plumbers, electrical contractors, PEs, inspectors, HVAC qualifiers). Each is placed as a bona fide officer or employee under a state-specific structure with real supervisory duties, E&O cover and indemnity. The service comes with (1) a lender-ready 'credential continuity package' (letter, duties, key-person plan), (2) a 12-month program that sponsors an internal successor through exams and hours, and (3) a state-by-state compliance library. It operates only in states where counsel confirms the qualifier rules allow this. License-lending schemes are illegal in many states, so compliance is the moat.
ideas.why_now: About 100 new US/Canadian search funds launched in 2023 (record), and acquisition volume grew from $110M to $880M per Stanford data summarized on Wikipedia. More than half of US small-business owners are 55+ without succession plans. PE Hub's September 2026 feed shows continuing PE appetite for HVAC, pest control and vet add-ons, which lifts what owners of licensed businesses expect to be paid and pulls more of them into sale processes. Buyer supply now exceeds credentialed-buyer supply.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-4K/month retainer per placement for 12-24 months. $1.5-2.5K one-time lender package. Sponsored successor-certification program billed at cost plus margin. Later, group E&O and key-person insurance placement commissions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint in trades acquisitions is the credential, not capital or price. Jack Rauch's Tew & Taylor deal was rejected by multiple banks because he had no building-code license or experience. Their words: 'you don't have this license, you don't have this experience... good luck. We won't touch it.' He had to close on family-office debt at a 33/33/33 cap table (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). Manolo Diaz Corrada's Bonneville deal names certifications as a single point of failure that take 'six months to a year to acquire' and are not economical to duplicate (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/manolo-diaz-corrada-bonneville-group). Nobody sells credential continuity as a product. Brokers treat it as the buyer's problem, and lenders treat it as a deal-killer.
